bib.title: Understanding Social Reasoning in Language Models with Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Understanding Social Reasoning in Language Models with Language Models" (BigToM). Kanishk Gandhi*, J.-Philipp Fränken*, Tobias Gerstenberg, Noah D. Goodman (*equal contribution). The only affiliation printed is "Stanford University". Venue as printed: "37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks." arXiv:2306.15448v2, 4 Dec 2023.

COVERAGE: 26 of 26 pages, 86,553 of 86,553 chars. That covers the main text, references and Appendices A–J including Tables 3–12. Nothing was skipped. Human accuracy for Forward Belief and Forward Action appears only as bars in Figs. 1 and 3, so I report no numbers for those.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- claim: Items are not written directly by the model. GPT-4 fills the variables of a causal template (context, desire, percept, belief, causal event, aware/unaware percepts, actions, questions, answers, random event), and code assembles each condition from them.
  number: 200 templates × 25 conditions = 5,000 items
  setup: gpt-4-0314, temperature 0.5, 3 completions per prompt from 3 few-shot examples, one sentence per variable; generation was fully autonomous
  quote: "In total, we generate 200 templates and extract 25 conditions from each template (resulting in a new benchmark consisting of 5,000 test items"
  where: p5 (§3.2–3.3); prompt on p13, Fig. 4

- claim: Crowd raters scored the generated items above crowd-written items and at or slightly above expert-written ones.
  number: aggregate contrast on a 1–5 Likert scale: BigToM − socialIQa 1.152; BigToM − Expert 0.263
  setup: 200 Prolific participants, 30 items each (20 BigToM, 5 Expert, 5 socialIQa), 20 ratings per item; 200 BigToM items against 50 socialIQa and 50 expert items; three questions (understandable, unambiguous, coherent Q&A); Bayesian mixed-effects model; preregistered. Only the Forward Belief true-belief and false-belief conditions were rated.
  quote: "“BigToM-socialIQa” , the estimate was 1.152 (95% CI: 1.066-1.244). For “BigToM-Expert”, the estimate was 0.263 (95% CI: 0.178 -0.347)"
  where: p14 (B.1); Table 3 on p15. The largest gap is on Unambiguous, 1.541 against socialIQa.

- claim: Two experts, who were also authors, checked the structure and validity of the items.
  number: 93.94% agreement on structure; means 0.919 and 0.960; "tests the desired behavior" 4.33 and 4.35 out of 5
  setup: 100 templates × 25 conditions (2,500 items)
  quote: "The overall percentage agreement between experts on the first question was 93.94% with mean ratings of 0.919 (95% CI: 0.859–0.970) for expert 1 and 0.960"
  where: p6 (§3.4)

- claim: False-belief success counts only when the model also passes the matched true-belief item. Otherwise a model could pass by never registering the change in the world.
  number: none
  setup: scoring rule "TB ∧ FB". Further controls are the with/without stated initial belief versions and a "Random Event" replacing the causal event (conditions 13–24).
  quote: "success on the false belief version of the task is evaluated only if the model succeeded on the true belief version, as otherwise a model might succeed on the false belief version for the wrong reasons"
  where: p7 (§4.1); p5; Fig. 6 on p15

- claim: GPT-4 is near ceiling on forward belief but far below humans on backward belief, zero-shot.
  number: GPT-4 TB∧FB zero-shot: Forward Belief .97/.90, Forward Action .79/.90, Backward Belief .40/.40 (without/with initial belief). Humans on Backward Belief: 82% TB, 72% FB.
  setup: temperature 0, two answer options; human baseline of 20 Prolific participants, "with initial belief" version only
  quote: "TB ∧ FB .40† .40‡" (Table 2, Bwd. Belief, 0-shot); "Even humans struggle, achieving only 82% accuracy in the true belief condition and 72% in the false belief condition."
  where: p8

- claim: Other models fail the critical conditions, and a stated initial belief anchors them.
  number: zero-shot Forward Action TB∧FB: gpt-3.5 .17/.20, claude-v1.3 .27/.42. On the random-event control the same gpt-3.5 cell is .77/.79.
  setup: Tables 7 and 8, zero-shot
  quote: "Fwd. Action TB ∧ FB .17† .20‡" (gpt-3.5)
  where: p21, p23

- claim: The authors tested the circularity worry by having a second model write a set.
  number: GPT-4 0.858 on the Claude-written set against 0.861 on its own; Claude-2 0.675 against 0.708; interaction b = −0.13, p = 0.620
  setup: BigToM-Claude, 30 templates / 750 items, against a size-matched subsample of BigToM
  quote: "Claude-2, despite generating BigToM-Claude performs worse than gpt-4 on this dataset."
  where: p22 (App. F); Table 10 on p24

- claim: Generation error rates are low, and weaker generators failed.
  number: about 3% common-sense errors (main text); 2–3% structure failures, rejected at parse time; 1–2% common-sense errors (App. C)
  setup: GPT-4. text-davinci-003 and gpt-3.5-turbo stayed unreliable even with staged generation plus verifier and reviser steps.
  quote: "gpt-4 occasionally fails to follow the structure of the template about 2-3% of the times."
  where: p17 (App. C); p9

- claim: One-shot chain-of-thought gains may reflect template mimicry.
  number: none
  quote: "mimicking the reasoning template is enough to solve our task in most cases"
  where: p8

LIMITS
- Conceded by the authors: "Our evaluation methodology may appear circular at first: the model being tested plays a role in generating the test items" (p8). They also concede content and stereotype bias from the generator, over-generation of some situations, syntactic similarity across items, and that "In domains where the models capabilities are lacking, the model will struggle to generate good evaluations" (p9).
- Not shown:
  - Crowd raters saw 2 of the 25 conditions. The hardest condition, Backward Belief, was not rated by crowd participants.
  - The expert raters were authors.
  - The human baseline has n=20 and covers one version.
  - The circularity check is 30 templates, with one alternate generator and no human-written set built from the same template.
  - The ~3% of erroneous items are not reported as removed from the released set.
  - Diversity (154 changeable states, 76 mechanisms, 7 perception media) was labelled by GPT-4 itself.
  - Items are two-option forced choice.
- Dated: the models are from 2023 (gpt-4-0314, claude-v1.3, claude-2, llama-65b quantized).
- Internal inconsistencies: the abstract says "25 controls", the body says 25 conditions. §4 says "five" models; footnote 3 and Table 7 list six.

BUILDS ON: Perez et al. [28] 2022, model-written evaluations. Dasgupta et al. [6] 2022, controlled tests and content effects. Baron-Cohen et al. [3] 1985 and Wimmer and Perner [46] 1983, false-belief tasks. Le et al. [21] 2019, ToMi templates. Sap et al. [32] 2019, socialIQa. Kosinski [18] 2023 and Ullman [42] 2023, expert items.

CODE: the condition recipe, Fig. 2a p4 / Fig. 6 p15:
"# 1 forward belief true
prior: {context} {desire} {action} {percept} {belief}
causal event: {causal event}
percept: {percept true belief}
question: {belief question}"

FIGURES: Figure 2, p4. "[a] Three-stage method for generating evaluations: Building a causal template for the domain (left). Creating a prompt template ... populating template variables using a language model (middle). Composing test items by combining template variables (right). [b] Crowdworker ratings ... compared to crowd-sourced ... and expert-written ToM evaluations." One image shows both the pipeline and its human validation.

PROBLEMS:
- Fig. 1 text extracts with the spaces stripped.
- The causal-graph icons in Tables 2, 7, 8 and 11 extract as stray `!` and `"`.
- Table 2 has a printed dagger typo (".54† .63†").
- No instructions aimed at the reader. The appendices contain generation and evaluation prompts and participant instructions, which I treated as data.
